title: Rank-four principal-minor conjecture for scaling matrices
statement:
Let $C\in\mathbb{C}^{d\times d}$ be a scaling matrix of rank four. A principal $4$-minor is **non-vanishing** when the corresponding principal submatrix has nonzero determinant. **Rank-four principal-minor conjecture.** The minimum number of non-vanishing principal $4$-minors is

$$
\binom{d-1}{3}.
$$

In particular, the corresponding delta-matroid lies in the orbit consisting of the families

$$
\mathcal{F}_\alpha=\{\emptyset\}\cup\binom{[d]}{2}\cup\binom{[d]}{3}\cup\mathcal{K}_\alpha,\qquad \alpha\in[d],
$$

where

$$
\mathcal{K}_\alpha=\left\{K\in\binom{[d]}{4}\mid\alpha\in K\right\}.
$$

Computations in the source support the claim in the examined small cases, but the general statement remains open.
references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16482

Status: **open** according to the source (as of June 2026). “While all delta-matroids appearing in Table admit such a realization, it remains open whether every delta-matroid on ground set $[6]$ is representable.”
source_name: Janike Oldekop, “Euler Stratifications of Second Hypersimplices via Delta-matroids”, arXiv:2606.16482 (2026).

progress.label: Open · solution reported
progress.tldr: A complete proof has been posted for the conjectured minimum, but it has not been independently verified, while published work confirms only small cases.
progress.summary:
The conjecture asserts that every rank-four scaling matrix has at least $\binom{d-1}{3}$ non-vanishing principal $4$-minors, with a stated equality characterization. It is attributed to Clarke et al. (2024), and the general claim was open in the latest primary source.

*[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16482)*

**Known results**

The primary source establishes the conjectured minimum for embeddings associated with second hypersimplices up to order six, but does not claim the general rank-four statement.


**Posted attempt**

An unverified complete proof reduces the problem to counting bases of a rank-four paving matroid, invokes a theorem of Chayim Lowen giving at least $\binom{d-1}{3}$ bases, characterizes equality, and supplies an equality construction for every $d\geq4$.

Current status (as of August 2026): Published work verifies only the examined small cases; a complete proof has been posted but not independently verified, so the general conjecture remains unsettled.

*Caveats. The posted argument may be correct, but no independent mathematical verification of its reduction, cited theorem application, and equality characterization was found.*

solutions.body:
Let \(C\) be a complex symmetric \(d\times d\) scaling matrix of rank \(4\), so \(C_{ii}=0\) and \(C_{ij}\neq0\) for \(i\neq j\). Choose a symmetric rank factorization
\[
C=XQX^{\mathsf T},
\]
where \(X\in\mathbb C^{d\times4}\) has full column rank and \(Q\in\mathbb C^{4\times4}\) is symmetric and invertible. For every four-element subset \(I\),
\[
\det C[I,I]=\det(Q)\det(X[I,:])^2. \tag{1}
\]
Hence the nonvanishing principal four-minors are exactly the bases of the rank-four row matroid of \(X\).

For every triple \(\{i,j,k\}\),
\[
\det C[\{i,j,k\},\{i,j,k\}]
=2C_{ij}C_{ik}C_{jk}\neq0.
\]
Thus every three rows of \(X\) are independent, and the represented matroid is paving.

We use the paving-matroid base theorem proved by Chayim Lowen: a rank-\(r\) paving matroid on \(d\) elements has at least
\[
\binom{d-1}{r-1}
\]
bases, with equality exactly for \(U_{r-1,d-1}\oplus U_{1,1}\). See the proof at https://mathoverflow.net/questions/412516/lower-bounds-for-the-number-of-bases-of-a-paving-matroid.

Applying this theorem with \(r=4\) and using (1) gives at least
\[
\binom{d-1}{3}
\]
nonzero principal four-minors. Equality holds exactly when some index \(\alpha\) is a coloop and the remaining \(d-1\) indices form \(U_{3,d-1}\), or equivalently exactly when the nonvanishing principal four-minors are those indexed by four-subsets containing \(\alpha\).

All principal two- and three-minors are nonzero, all principal one-minors vanish, and every principal minor of order at least five vanishes. Consequently the equality-case delta-matroid is precisely
\[
\mathcal F_\alpha
=\{\varnothing\}\cup\binom{[d]}2\cup\binom{[d]}3
\cup\{I\in\binom{[d]}4:\alpha\in I\}.
\]

Finally, equality is attained for every \(d\geq4\). Put \(m=d-1\), let
\[
D_{ij}=(i-j)^2\quad(1\leq i,j\leq m),\qquad
u=D\mathbf1,\qquad
C=\begin{pmatrix}D&u\\u^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Every off-diagonal entry of \(C\) is strictly positive. Writing \(t=(1,\ldots,m)^{\mathsf T}\), we have
\[
D=t^{\circ2}\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}
-2tt^{\mathsf T}
+\mathbf1(t^{\circ2})^{\mathsf T},
\]
so \(\operatorname{rank}D\leq3\). Every three-element principal minor equals
\[
2(i-j)^2(i-k)^2(j-k)^2\neq0,
\]
and therefore \(\operatorname{rank}D=3\). Because \(u=D\mathbf1\), block congruence gives
\[
C\sim\operatorname{diag}
\left(D,-\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}D\mathbf1\right),
\]
and \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}D\mathbf1>0\); hence \(\operatorname{rank}C=4\). The first \(m\) indices have matroid rank three, every triple among them is independent, and the final index is a coloop. Thus exactly
\[
\binom{d-1}{3}
\]
principal four-minors are nonzero. This proves both the sharp bound and its complete equality characterization.
